## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: false
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).

## Assembly overview

r code chunk that tabulates the alignment statistics

```{r}
alignment_statistics <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c(
    "Total length",
    "N50",
    "Number of contigs",
    "Largest contig",
    "coverage"
   ),
  Results = c(
    10200725,
    28892,
    431,
    85071,
    6
  )
)
alignment_statistics
```

Looking at alignment statistics, we can not expect a complete genome as total genome of about 10.2 million base pairs is divided into 431 fragments. Also, mean coverage of 6x is very low as Flye requires at least 15x to 20x coverage to find overlaps, repeats and construct high quality consensus sequence.

## Evaluating assembly using BUSCO

### BUSCO Scores

C:42.7%\[S:42.7%,D:0.1%\],F:0.7%,M:56.6%,n:3282,E:6.6%

Since Flye mean coverage was 6x, the above given BUSCO score makes sense. Only 42.7% of genes were found in their total length while 56.5% of genome was missing because Flye could not assemble it.Low F (fragmented) score of 0.7% suggests that genes were not truncated, either reads were assembled or missed completely.

### BUSCO N50

Scaffold N50 = 28 kbp Contigs N50 = 28 kbp

The N50 is approximately equal to Flye N50 of 28892

### Total Assembly length

Total assembly length is 10032501

## Evaluating assembly using QUAST

### Genome Fraction

Genome fraction is 4.917%. Genome Fraction is based on the fact that how much of the particular reference genome matches assembly while BUSCO tells how many important genes were recovered

### Duplication ratio

Duplication ratio is 1.017

### Misassemblies

Number of misassemblies is 1 and length of misassembled contigs is 18,084. This suggests that regions of strain assembly that could be aligned to S.cerevisiae reference were structurally consistent with it.

## Garbing the longest cotig

code chunk to extract the longest contig

```{r}
# load required packages 
library(Biostrings)

# Read contigs
readContigs <- readDNAStringSet("outputs/medaka_round2/consensus.fasta")

# Find longest contig
longest <- which.max(width(readContigs))

# Extract longest contig 
longest_contig <- readContigs[longest]

# write to new fasta file
writeXStringSet(longest_contig, "outputs/longest_contig.fasta")
```


## Aligning CDSs to the longest contig

code chunk that converts cds_aln.sam file to a sorted and indexed BAM file for visualization

```{bash}
samtools view -bS outputs/cds_aln.sam > outputs/cds_alignment.bam
samtools sort outputs/cds_alignment.bam -o outputs/cds_aln.sorted.bam
samtools index outputs/cds_aln.sorted.bam
```


## Visualizing CDSs

```{r}
# BAM file path
bam_file1 <- "outputs/cds_aln.sorted.bam"

# Open connection to BAM file
bam1 <- BamFile(bam_file1)

# Read all alignments
alns1 <- readGAlignments(bam1)

# Convert to GRanges object
gr_alns1 <- granges(alns1)

# Find the start and end boundaries of all mapped contigs combined
range(gr_alns1)

# set to false
options(ucscChromosomeNames=FALSE)

# Create tracks showing alignment
aln_track1 <- AlignmentsTrack("outputs/cds_aln.sorted.bam", isPaired = FALSE)

# Add genome axis for scale
axis_track1 <- GenomeAxisTrack()

# Visualize the alignment
# Plot
plotTracks(list(axis_track1, aln_track1),
           from = min(start(gr_alns1)),
           to = max(end(gr_alns1)),
           chromosome = "contig_301",
           main = "CDSs Alignments to Chromosome 1")

# reset to true
options(ucscChromosomeNames=TRUE)
```
